title: Olympiad Day 2: Big guns enter arena in Samarkand
summary: The leading teams field their strongest line-ups as Samarkand delivers another fascinating day of chess. Round two of the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand brought many of the world’s leading players into action, as the top seeds largely decided that it was time to put their strongest line-ups on the board. With the first points already secured, the focus shifted to maintaining momentum, although several matches proved considerably more competitive than the ratings suggested. From impressive debuts by established stars to a few unexpected results and some spectacular tactical finishes, there was plenty to keep the packed playing hall entertained. Let’s take a closer look at the action from the playing hall. Two ceremonial first moves were performed today. On board one of the Open section match between the United States of America and Mongolia, Mohamed Al Mudahka, FIDE Technical Delegate and President of the Qatar Chess Federation, made the symbolic opening move 1.d4. A few moments later, Komil Sindarov, Vice President of the Uzbekistan Chess Federation, also opened with 1.d4 in the Women’s top-board encounter between Finland and India. Although the second-round pairings were not expected to produce too many upsets, few teams were willing to rest their top players for a second consecutive day. As a result, spectators who flocked to the playing hall for the start of the round were treated to the debuts of some of the best players in the world. The challenger to the upcoming World Championship match, Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov, led his team to a convincing 3.5–0.5 victory over the young Peruvian squad. Checkmate of the dayFlores Quillas – Javokhir Sindarov Sindarov had played a virtually perfect game up to this point, registering an outstanding 98% accuracy. His extra pawn should have been more than enough to secure the win – 31…Qa1, for example, comes to mind. But the challenger wanted to make a statement. Instead, he uncorked the fantastic 31…Kf7!!, sacrificing his queen for the second time in the game. Flores Quillas could perhaps have resigned at this point but elegantly accepted the gift with 32.Qxf1. This allowed Sindarov to complete the combination with 32…Rh3!!, threatening a spectacular checkmate with 33…h6! The mate can be delayed, but not prevented. Fabiano Caruana made his debut on board one for the USA with a powerful performance against Mongolia’s Sumiya Bilguun. Combined with Levon Aronian’s narrow win and Hans Niemann’s solid draw, the result was enough to secure the match victory despite a major surprise on board four. There, Awonder Liang, rated 2693, was defeated by Khuyagtsogt Itgelt, rated 2435. Playing White, the Mongolian produced an outstanding performance, beautifully punishing Liang’s risky choice of the Benoni and completely dismantling his opponent’s position. Defending champions India had a tough outing against Indonesia, who put up determined resistance throughout the match. Three draws, with Gukesh, Vidit and Praggnanandhaa all held to half a point, were compensated by Nihal Sarin’s fantastic lone win, allowing India to remain among the leading teams in the standings. One of the heroes of the match was Indonesian teenager Satria Duta, who held reigning World Champion Gukesh to a draw. Delighted with his result, the young Indonesian happily agreed to an interview with Charlize van Zyl. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KS1VjCcvo8M China’s board one, former World Champion Ding Liren, has been fielded in both of the first two rounds. After winning yesterday, he was held to a draw today by Chile’s Rodrigo Vásquez Schroeder, having miscalculated in what had been a very promising position. Fortunately for China, Wei Yi made his debut on board two at just the right moment. The Chinese star produced a fantastic performance, featuring a trademark exchange sacrifice, to help his team secure an important 3–1 victory over Chile. Ding Liren also shared his thoughts on China’s prospects in Samarkand in his post-game interview. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=spCHbOtF-3s World number six Vincent Keymer, 21, made his debut for Germany this afternoon with a smooth positional grind against Saidakbar Saydaliev of Uzbekistan 3. Tactic of the dayVincent Keymer – Saidakbar Saydaliev Black was under pressure but could have kept the game going with a move such as 30…Bb7. Instead, Saydaliev lashed out with 30…g5, attempting to drive the knight away, but was immediately punished by the tactical 31.Nxe6! After 31…Rxe6 (31…Nxe6 would lose to 32.Rxc6) Keymer continued with 32.Bxe6+ Kxe6, reaching the key moment of the combination. The German star then found the beautiful 33.Bc7!, after which his opponent resigned. The point is that either knight or bishop cannot be saved, leaving Black with no way to avoid losing material. Germany won the match by a clear 3.5–0.5. Their opponents, Uzbekistan 3, are a young team of promising prospects, all born between 2001 and 2008.As the host nation, Uzbekistan has the right to field two teams instead of one, while a third team is frequently added when the total number of teams is uneven. In a post-game interview with Charlize van Zyl, Keymer said he enjoys team events and was pleased with the chemistry within the German squad. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=il2ts_ypDEY Other leading teams, including the Netherlands, Azerbaijan, France, Armenia, England, Ukraine, Poland and Spain, also came through with victories, although several of them dropped a point or point and a half along the way. Whereas the leading teams in the Open section are already beginning to lose points here and there, the Women’s section is still producing some emphatic 4–0 victories at the top of the standings. Local favorites Uzbekistan crushed Ecuador with relatively quick wins on all four boards, recording exactly the same score as the United States of America in their match against Belgium. Both 17-year-old Afruza Khamdamova and 23-year-old Carissa Yip made their Samarkand debuts on board one and marked the occasion with convincing victories. Seed number three, Kazakhstan, however, had to settle for a 3–1 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina. On board one, Milana Babić held debutant Bibisara Assaubayeva to a draw. And no doubt the upset of the day was Montenegro’s 2-2 tie against seed number two Georgia, mainly due to Alena Skvortsova

title: Poland crowned champions as Samarkand Olympiad for People with Disabilities concludes with a celebration of chess and inclusion
summary: Seven days of competition, a record 41 teams and countless stories from across the chess world came to a close in Samarkand, as Poland claimed gold at the 3rd FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities. Cuba finished with silver, while hosts Uzbekistan 1 secured bronze on a memorable final day. Round 7 began with FIDE Interim President and five-time World Champion Viswanathan Anand making the ceremonial first move before the final battles got underway. Poland entered the last round at the top of the standings and left no room for doubt, defeating the Philippines 3½–½. IM Marcin Molenda drew Menandro Redor on the top board, while IM Pawel Piekielny, IM Aleksander Czerwonski and Julia Salamon scored victories to complete a commanding final-round performance. The result brought Poland to 13 match points, completing an undefeated campaign of six victories and one draw and securing the title of the 3rd FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities. Behind them, the battle for the podium came down to the wire. Cuba defeated the Czech Republic 2½–1½ to finish on 12 match points and take silver, while Uzbekistan 1 overcame Israel by the same 2½–1½ margin to score 11 match points and earn bronze in front of the home crowd. Poland finishes on top For Polish captain IM Marcin Molenda, the gold medal was the culmination of a tournament that had not started according to plan. After dropping a point in the opening round, Poland responded by winning every remaining match. “It was definitely a rollercoaster. The first round, losing the points. After that, winning every single match. So, I’m quite happy, especially with the team, since we managed to pull this off.” For Molenda, the significance of Samarkand went beyond the gold medal, with the Olympiad for People with Disabilities held alongside the main FIDE Chess Olympiad for the first time. “Historically, we were playing some separate events. So right now, being with all the top players, grandmasters and also the world champions as well, is very important for us.” He also praised the team’s experience in Uzbekistan: “It was fantastic. The opening ceremony, as well as the closing ceremony, showed us a lot of culture, a lot of interesting facts about Uzbekistan. And also, it shows a really huge interest in chess.” The final podium:  Gold – Poland (13 match points)Silver – Cuba (12 match points)Bronze – Uzbekistan 1 (11 match points) Poland’s success was also reflected in the individual awards, with Marcin Molenda, Pawel Piekielny, and Aleksander Czerwonski all collecting individual board medals. Friends from the wider chess family The final day also brought a special visit from the Czech chess community. GM David Navara and Petr Boleslav, organiser of the Prague Chess Festival, came to the Olympiad, met with participants, and shared in the atmosphere of the final day. Their visit added another warm connection between the participants of the Olympiad for People with Disabilities and the wider chess community gathered in Samarkand. Another special guest was Ukrainian grandmaster Vasyl Ivanchuk, who also visited the Olympiad and spent time with the participants. The presence of one of the most recognisable figures in international chess added another memorable moment to the final day, as the event welcomed players and guests from the wider chess world before the competition came to a close. From one Olympiad to another Molenda’s words reflected one of the defining features of this year’s event. Once the final games were over, that connection became even more tangible, as participants of the Olympiad for People with Disabilities had the opportunity to visit the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad. Players and team members explored the Expo, enjoyed the atmosphere of the main event and watched players from around the world competing in the Open and Women’s sections. For the first time, the FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities was staged alongside the main FIDE Chess Olympiad in the same host city and during the same period. With their own seven-round competition complete, participants could move directly into the atmosphere of the main Olympiad – sharing the same chess environment and becoming part of a much larger celebration of the game. A home medal for Uzbekistan For the hosts, the final round brought another reason to celebrate. Selbi Kakishova helped Uzbekistan 1 secure the team bronze while also earning an individual silver medal on Board 5, having scored an impressive six points from seven games. “The tournament was so exciting. I’m so happy. On my board, from seven games, I won six games, and that’s why I got silver. Overall, our team took bronze.” The seven rounds had not been easy, but Kakishova felt the effort had paid off. “All the games were so hard and difficult, but despite that, I gave all my strength, and that’s why we won.” For Kakishova, competing at home while the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad was also getting underway in Samarkand provided additional motivation. “It was so exciting. A few days ago, there was the opening, and during the opening, I got a lot of motivation, and that’s why I also gave all my strength.” Medals, music, and celebration In the evening, players, officials, and guests came together for the closing ceremony, bringing seven days of competition to a festive end with music, songs, and dances, followed by the presentation of the team, individual, and special awards. Uzbekistan 1 received the bronze medals, Cuba took silver, while newly crowned champions Poland stepped onto the podium to receive gold. Individual medals were also presented across all five boards. The board winners were FM Sargis Sargissyan (IPCA) on Board 1, IM Pawel Piekielny (Poland) on Board 2, IM Aleksander Czerwonski (Poland) on Board 3, Darry Bernardo (Philippines) on Board 4 and Michal Racis (IBCA) on Board 5. A series of special prizes, presented by Dana Reizniece, Acting Chair of the FIDE Management Board, completed the awards ceremony, recognising players from across the diverse field of the Olympiad. Addressing the participants, Viswanathan Anand congratulated the winners

title: Freedom Holding Corp. backs FIDE World Championship Match 2026 as General Partner
summary: The International Chess Federation (FIDE) and Freedom Holding Corp. (NASDAQ: FRHC) announced today that Freedom has become the General Partner of the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026.  The match will take place from 22 November to 12 December in Switzerland. The opening ceremony will be held on 22 November at the Palais des Nations in Geneva. World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju of India defends his title against Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan over 14 classical games. Both players will be twenty at the start of the match, the youngest title contest since the competition began in 1886. Freedom has been a strategic partner of FIDE since 2023. The group is a regular sponsor of the FIDE World Rapid and Blitz Championships and was the title sponsor of the 2024 FIDE World Corporate Chess Championship in New York. Under the 2026 cooperation agreement, Freedom also funds FIDE tournaments, training centers, school programmes and talent scouting across all continents. The World Championship extends that partnership to the sport’s defining event. The championship sponsorship reflects how Freedom approaches the game: as a system to be built over years, from the classroom to the championship board. “The World Championship decides who is first. There is nothing bigger in chess,” said Timur Turlov, founder and CEO of Freedom Holding Corp., President of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, and head of the International School Chess Federation, the regulating body for chess in education. “Freedom has worked with FIDE for three years, and this is the natural next step, not a logo on a stage. Chess and finance are the same discipline: you calculate, you decide under uncertainty, you refuse the obvious move, and you plan far ahead. We invest in chess on that horizon,” he added. “Freedom has committed to chess seriously, over years and at every level of the game,” said Viswanathan Anand, five-time World Champion and FIDE Interim President. “To have them behind a World Championship contested by two twenty-year-olds is fitting. This company understands chess is a long game, and this Match is its future.”  “The World Championship is the pinnacle of chess,” said Emil Sutovsky, CEO of FIDE. “It is the event that decides who stands first. We are proud to have support of Freedom – a company that champions smart solutions and has a long-term vision, calculating moves ahead much like top chess players.” About Freedom Holding Corp.Freedom Holding Corp. (NASDAQ: FRHC) is a U.S.-listed diversified financial and technology group headquartered in Kazakhstan, operating brokerage, banking, insurance, telecommunications and lifestyle services in more than twenty countries. A strategic partner of FIDE since 2023, Freedom treats chess as a long-horizon cultural and educational investment. About FIDEThe International Chess Federation (FIDE), founded in 1924 and headquartered in Switzerland, is the governing body of world chess and organiser of the World Championship cycle.
